explanations.answer: The whole earth east to west
explanations.explanation: Asaph says God summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets. That covers every address on the map, friend. Even the guy who never opens his mail is on this list. When the Mighty One calls, nobody gets skipped.

Asaph doesn't name priests here. He says God summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets. A temple only holds so many folks, and this summons is way bigger than any building. It reaches from one horizon to the other.
Not quite, friend. The psalm doesn't mention kings in this verse. It says God summons the earth from sunrise to sunset. I'd say kings are included in that, but so is everybody else.

Not quite. Asaph says the opposite: "Our God approaches and will not be silent!" Then he adds that consuming fire goes before Him and a tempest rages around Him. That is no tiptoeing. When God shows up, everybody knows it.

Right, friend. Asaph says "Our God approaches and will not be silent!" He also says consuming fire goes before Him, and a tempest rages around Him. Nothing quiet about that arrival. I've never seen a bakery door open with that much fire and wind, and I hope I never do.

explanations.answer: So He can judge His people
explanations.explanation: Yes! Asaph says God summons the heavens above and the earth "that He may judge His people." The call has a purpose, and the text tells us what it is. He isn't gathering folks for a stroll. He's gathering them so His people stand before Him as Judge.

explanations.answer: So He can build His temple
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The psalm doesn't say anything about building. It says God summons the heavens and the earth "that He may judge His people." Judging is the whole reason for the call.

explanations.answer: So He can make them new
explanations.explanation: Close to a good thought, but not what the verse says. God making things new does show up elsewhere in the Bible (Revelation 21:5). Here Asaph says God summons the heavens and the earth "that He may judge His people." Judging is the purpose in this verse.
That's it! The call says, “Gather to Me My saints, who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice.” Gathered to Him, friend. Not scattered, not sent off somewhere. Close to Him.
Not quite. The call doesn't send anybody out. It says, “Gather to Me My saints, who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice.” These saints are being brought in, not sent away.
Not this one, friend. The call says nothing about priests. It says, “Gather to Me My saints, who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice.” The call is about gathering them to God.
Yes, friend. Asaph says, "And the heavens proclaim His righteousness, for God Himself is Judge." The heavens are announcing it. Then comes a Selah, a pause in the song, so we can let it sink in.
Not quite. Asaph says the heavens proclaim His righteousness, "for God Himself is Judge." The sky is doing the announcing. All that's left for us is to listen.

Not quite, friend. God says, "I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, and your burnt offerings are ever before Me." So the sacrifices aren't the problem. His complaint is coming from somewhere else, and we'll get there.

Right. God says, "I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, and your burnt offerings are ever before Me." They're not in trouble over the offerings. It's like a boss saying, "Your work is fine," and then pulling up a chair for a different talk.

explanations.answer: Every beast of the forest is His
explanations.explanation: There it is! God says, "for every beast of the forest is Mine—the cattle on a thousand hills." You can't hand somebody what already belongs to Him. That's like bringing me a bag of flour from my own pantry and saying, "Surprise!"
Not quite, friend. God doesn't ask for grain here. He says every beast of the forest is His, and the cattle on a thousand hills. That's why He has no need for a bull or goats from His people.

The text doesn't say that, friend. God says, "I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices." His reason is that every beast of the forest is His, and the cattle on a thousand hills. Nothing in these verses says anything was wrong with the animals.
Yes! God says, "If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof." The whole world, and everything in it. He's not short on anything, friend.
Not the word, friend. God says, "for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof." The whole world, not one building in it. His reach goes way past any temple.
Close, but no. God says the world is His, and the fullness thereof. The verse doesn't mention a throne. The world is bigger than any chair, even a very fancy one.

That's it! God says, "Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High." He owns everything, so what He asks for is thanks. And I'll tell you, thanks is a gift I never get tired of getting.
Not quite, friend. God has the cattle on a thousand hills, so a bigger herd wouldn't add anything. What He says is, "Sacrifice a thank offering to God." He wants thanks, not more animals.

explanations.answer: A gift of gold and silver
explanations.explanation: Not this time. In this psalm God asks for a thank offering, not gold and silver. Haggai 2:8 says the silver and the gold are His too. He's the owner of the whole world, so what He asks for is thanks.
Yes! God says, "Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor Me." Day of trouble, call on Him, and He delivers. Simple as that, friend.
Not the word, friend. God says, "Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you." The promise is that He will deliver them. The verse doesn't say anything about testing.
Not quite. Teaching is a fine thing, but that's not what God promises here. He says, "I will deliver you, and you will honor Me." A day of trouble gets rescue.
Yes, friend. God says, "For you hate My instruction and cast My words behind you." They can say the words and still not want them. Knowing the lines and loving the Lord are two different things.

explanations.answer: They add rules of their own
explanations.explanation: Not quite. God never says that here. He says, "For you hate My instruction and cast My words behind you." The problem is how they treat His words, not extra rules.

explanations.answer: They recite them only in private
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't say that, friend. God asks, "What right have you to recite My statutes and to bear My covenant on your lips?" Then He says, "you hate My instruction." The trouble He names is hating His instruction.
Yes, friend. God says, "When you see a thief, you befriend him, and throw in your lot with adulterers." The wicked don't turn away from a thief. They pull up a chair next to him.
Not quite. God says, "When you see a thief, you befriend him, and throw in your lot with adulterers." So it's friendship, not distance. That's what He's calling out.
Yes. God says, "You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother’s son." It's family, friend. Slandering a stranger is bad enough, and this is somebody from their own home.
Not this one. God doesn't mention prophets here. He says, "You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother’s son." The person being slandered is their brother.
Not quite, friend. The psalm doesn't mention a king in these verses. God says, "You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother’s son." The target is their own brother.

explanations.answer: That He was just like them
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says, "you thought I was just like you." They took His silence to mean He was the same as they were. I bet that thought felt comfortable for a while. Then comes, "But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face."
The text doesn't say that, friend. God says, "You have done these things, and I kept silent; you thought I was just like you." Their mistake was thinking He was like them. And then He rebukes them.
Not quite. God says they thought He was "just like you." The psalm doesn't say they thought He was far off. It says He kept silent and they drew the wrong conclusion about who He is.
Not quite, friend. God says, "But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face." The silence ends. He's speaking, and He's speaking straight to them.
Right. God says, "You have done these things, and I kept silent… But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face." The quiet part is over. He's talking now, face to face.
Yes! God says, "He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me." That's a lovely line, friend. Thanks given to God honors Him.
Not the word, friend. God says, "He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me." Earlier He said He needs nothing from them. So the word is honors, not repays.
Not quite. God says the one who sacrifices a thank offering "honors Me." Nobody's in debt in this verse. A thank offering honors Him.
Yes! God says, "to him who rightly orders his way, I will show the salvation of God." After all that heavy warning, the psalm ends with a promise. And it's the best one on the list, friend.

explanations.answer: A long life in the land
explanations.explanation: Not quite. A long life in the land isn't what this verse says. God says, "to him who rightly orders his way, I will show the salvation of God." The last promise is salvation.
Not this one, friend. Riches aren't mentioned in these verses. God says, "to him who rightly orders his way, I will show the salvation of God." He ends the psalm with salvation, not wealth.
